results.title: Interactive peacebuilding workshops delivered by ILRI to equip youth with conflict resolution skills in Ethiopia and Mali
results.description: Young people in pastoral and rural communities across Ethiopia and Mali often lack platforms to voice concerns about resource-related conflicts and skills to address these challenges constructively. The International Livestock Research Institute developed and delivered interactive dialogue workshops specifically targeting youth in these regions. The workshops equipped participants with practical tools for conflict resolution and peacebuilding related to natural resource management, while ensuring development interventions remain sensitive to local conflicts. These sessions created safe spaces for youth to share perspectives on community challenges and develop locally-relevant solutions. By empowering young voices in peacebuilding processes, this capacity-building initiative contributes to more inclusive development approaches that strengthen social cohesion in pastoral communities across both countries.

results.title: Key Drivers of Improved Nitrogen Use Efficiency in Intensive Wheat Systems in Egypt
results.description: Excessive use of fertilizers and water, common in intensive farming systems, has led to diminishing returns, environmental degradation, increasing soil salinity, and increased production costs. In Egypt’s intensively cultivated irrigated drylands, average nitrogen use efficiency under farmers’ management is below 30%, indicating substantial losses of applied nitrogen. It is therefore crucial to develop and promote context-specific management practices that improve nutrient use efficiency, sustain agricultural production, and reduce environmental impacts, while identifying the main drivers of improved efficiency. This study shows that planting method (raised beds with furrow irrigation), phosphorus application rate, use of quality seed, organic matter inputs, variety choice, sowing time, number of tillage passes, and water management are key drivers for enhancing nitrogen use efficiency in intensified wheat systems

results.title: Multiplex PCR for detection of AMV and SBMV was optimized
results.description: The aim is to optimize and avail cost effective and efficient disease diagnostic tool that detects multiple pathogens at a time. A multiplex PCR (m-PCR) assay was successfully optimized to enable simultaneous detection of two important seedborne viruses (AMV and SBMV) in forage crops, offering a more efficient alternative to conventional single-target diagnostic methods. Using reference controls and field and greenhouse samples, the assay conditions was optimized and validated using 30 samples . The result showed strong agreement with conventional RT-PCR results, demonstrating the reliability of the method. The optimized m-PCR provides a rapid, sensitive, and cost-effective tool that can enhance routine virus indexing, seed health testing, and phytosanitary monitoring in forage and legume production systems.

results.title: A one health approach to address foodborne diseases in low‑ and middle‑income countries
results.description: Foodborne diseases (FBDs) are defined as any diseases that result from the ingestion of contaminated or naturally hazardous food [1]. Health outcomes due to FBDs lead to more than 100 million USD of annual preventable economic burden, and over 90% of these economic losses occur in low‑ and middle‑income countries (LMICs) [2]. FBDs disproportionately impact children under 5 years of age. Representing only 9% of the global population, they experience detrimental health outcomes including 38% of all FBD incidence and as much as 30% of premature mortality [3]. Stunting and wasting are pernicious consequences of FBDs among children under 5 years of age. Africa and South‑East Asia have the highest FBD incidence and mortality. Although 41% of the global population are poor, they account for 75% of FBD‑related premature mortality and a 72% loss in global disability‑adjusted life years (DALYs) [3]. In LMICs, FBDs arise primarily owing to the interconnected issues of dwindling animal and plant health, food systems vulnerable to contaminations, and food pathogens and zoonotic threats [1, 2, 4]. There has been a dramatic upsurge in urbanization in LMICs. This trend has accompanied dietary shifts. For example, there is an increase in consumption of animal products (the foods with the highest FBD risk) and intensively managed farming systems. Further, simple food value chains have been supplanted with complex food systems with little traceability. It is now widely acknowledged that human health is intricately linked with animal health, along with our shared ecosystem. The reduction of FBDs, thus, demands a unified framework that pays concurrent attention to the health of humans, animals, and the shared environment. This merits increased attention to adopting a One Health (OH) approach to address FBDs, and by extension, contributing to food security.

results.title: Technical Support and Capacity Building for Mali-Météo in Data Sharing Tool (DST) and Enhancing National Climate Services initiative (ENACTS)
results.description: This deliverable built the capacity building provided of Mali-Météo for deploying the Data Sharing Tool (DST) and ENACTS tools. ENACTS addresses gaps in climate data by integrating ground observations with satellite data to create high-quality, spatially complete datasets, while DST tailored to Mali-Météo’s needs, enables secure, selective data sharing. Six staff members, including two women, were trained in the use of DST and ENACTS. The capacity building focuses on understanding the structure of the DST and ENACTS training, enhancing Mali-Météo ability to upgrade weather and climate data and share with stakeholders for informed decision making.

results.title: Root penetration is associated with root diameter and root growth rate in tropical forage grasses
results.description: Soil compaction impedes root exploration by plants, which limits access to nutrients and water, ultimately compromising survival. The capability of roots to penetrate hard soils is therefore advantageous. While root penetration has been studied in various annual crops, the relationships between root growth and root penetration are poorly understood in tropical perennial grasses. This study aimed to compare root penetration capability in 10 tropical perennial forage grasses and identify relationships between root penetration, root diameter and vertical root growth. Root penetration of each species, namely Urochloa (syn. Brachiaria) brizantha cv. Mekong Briz, U. decumbens cv. Basilisk, U. humidicola cv. Tully, U. hybrid cv. Mulato II, U. mosambicensis cv. Nixon, U. ruziziensis cv Kennedy, Panicum coloratum cv. Makarikariense, Megathyrsus maximus (syn. Panicum maximum) cv. Tanzânia, Paspalum scrobiculatum (syn. Paspalum coloratum) cv. BA96 10 and Setaria sphacelata cv Solendar, was evaluated using wax layers of varying resistances, created from a mixture of 40% (1.39 MPa) and 60% (2.12 MPa) paraffin wax, combined with petroleum jelly. Reference root sizes were determined for the grass species by measuring root diameter and root lengths of seedlings grown in growth pouches. Vertical root growth rate for each species was measured in grasses grown in 120 cm deep rhizotrons. Species with greater root penetration at both resistances had significantly higher shoot growth rates (r = 0.65 at 40% wax and 0.66 at 60% wax) and greater root diameters (r = 0.67 at 40% wax and 0.68 at 60% wax). Root penetration was significantly higher in species with greater vertical root growth rate only in the 60% wax treatment (r = 0.82). Root penetration at higher resistance was correlated with the root diameter and rapid vertical root growth of the species. This may indicate a contribution of these traits to root penetration ability. The combination of greater root diameter and root vertical growth rate, as observed in M. maximus, may assist in the identification of perennial forage grasses suitable for agroecosystems challenged by soil compaction and rapidly drying soil surface.

results.title: Lineamientos para el manejo agronómico y fitosanitario de las variedades de papa biofortificadas CIP–KALLPA YAWRI y CIP–PUKA YAWRI en zonas altoandinas del Perú
results.description:
El Centro Internacional de la Papa (CIP) desarrolló las variedades biofortificadas CIP–KALLPA YAWRI y CIP–PUKA YAWRI con el objetivo de contribuir a la reducción de la anemia en poblaciones altoandinas. Estas variedades, liberadas oficialmente en 2024 y 2025, contienen entre 35% y 55% más hierro que las variedades tradicionales y presentan resistencia comprobada al tizón tardío, lo que disminuye la necesidad de fungicidas. Su desempeño agronómico ha sido validado en 26 localidades de la sierra norte, centro y sur del Perú entre 2018 y 2021, mostrando buena adaptación entre los 2 600 y más de 4 000 m s.n.m. y rendimientos promedio de 25 t/ha.
Los lineamientos propuestos orientan el manejo de estas variedades en condiciones altoandinas. Se recomienda seleccionar terrenos con suelos sueltos, bien drenados y con buen contenido de materia orgánica, así como planificar la siembra entre octubre y mayo según el régimen de lluvias. El uso de semilla certificada es ideal; sin embargo, en sistemas familiares se puede recurrir a la selección positiva. Las labores agronómicas incluyen dos aporques oportunos, control manual de malezas y una fertilización ajustada al análisis de suelo, tomando como referencia una dosis de 180–180–160 kg/ha de N–P₂O₅–K₂O.
La cosecha se realiza alrededor de los 145 días después de la siembra, pudiendo variar por altitud. Se recomienda eliminar el follaje un par de semanas antes para uniformizar la madurez y mejorar la calidad del tubérculo. Las prácticas adecuadas de curado y almacenamiento son esenciales para preservar su calidad y viabilidad como semilla o producto de consumo.
El manejo fitosanitario se centra en la prevención y el monitoreo continuo, dado que, aunque las variedades son resistentes al tizón tardío, aún pueden verse afectadas por otras enfermedades y plagas frecuentes en zonas altoandinas, incluyendo gorgojo de los Andes, polilla de la papa, pulguilla saltona, mosca minadora, pulgones y el psílido de la papa. Se enfatiza la rotación de cultivos, la eliminación de residuos y el uso racional de productos químicos solo cuando sea estrictamente necesario, complementando con control biológico cuando corresponda.
En conjunto, estos lineamientos buscan asegurar un manejo sostenible y eficiente de CIP–KALLPA YAWRI y CIP–PUKA YAWRI, potenciando su impacto nutricional y productivo, y contribuyendo al bienestar de las familias rurales de los Andes del Perú.

results.title_en: Guidelines for the agronomic and phytosanitary management of the biofortified potato varieties CIP–KALLPA YAWRI and CIP–PUKA YAWRI in high-Andean zones of Peru
results.description_en:
The International Potato Center (CIP) developed the biofortified varieties CIP–KALLPA YAWRI and CIP–PUKA YAWRI aiming to help reduce anemia in high-Andean populations. These varieties, officially released in 2024 and 2025, contain between 35% and 55% more iron than traditional varieties and have proven resistance to late blight, reducing the need for fungicides. Their agronomic performance was validated in 26 locations in the northern, central, and southern highlands of Peru between 2018 and 2021, showing good adaptation between 2,600 and over 4,000 m a.s.l. and average yields of 25 t/ha.

The proposed guidelines direct the management of these varieties under high-Andean conditions. It is recommended to select fields with loose, well-drained soils and good organic matter content, and to plan planting between October and May according to the rainfall regime. Use of certified seed is ideal; however, in family systems positive selection can be used. Agronomic operations include two timely hilling (aporques), manual weed control, and fertilization adjusted to soil analysis, taking as a reference a dose of 180–180–160 kg/ha of N–P2O5–K2O.

Harvest is carried out at around 145 days after planting, which can vary by altitude. It is recommended to remove foliage a couple of weeks before harvest to uniformize maturity and improve tuber quality. Proper curing and storage practices are essential to preserve quality and viability as seed or as a food product.

Phytosanitary management focuses on prevention and continuous monitoring, since although the varieties are resistant to late blight, they can still be affected by other diseases and pests common in high-Andean areas, including Andean weevil, potato tuber moth, flea beetles, leafminer fly, aphids, and potato psyllid. Crop rotation, residue removal, and rational use of chemical products only when strictly necessary are emphasized, complemented by biological control where appropriate.

Together, these guidelines aim to ensure sustainable and efficient management of CIP–KALLPA YAWRI and CIP–PUKA YAWRI, enhancing their nutritional and productive impact and contributing to the well-being of rural families in the Peruvian Andes.

results.title: Congress with agricultural stakeholders and civil society representatives to advance solutions and compliance with the EU Deforestation Regulation
results.description: From 2–4 September 2025, the Congreso EUDR&Data 2025 brought together approximately 250 participants from across the public and private sectors, producer organizations, technical partners, and civil society to advance practical and scalable solutions for data management and compliance with the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR). The congress was organized under the Team Europe Initiative on Deforestation-Free Value Chains, co-financed by the European Union and the German Federal Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation, Nuclear Safety and Consumer Protection (BMUV), and convened by GIZ in collaboration with PROMECAFE, Bioversity International + CIAT, and COSA. The event emphasized co-creation and shared learning on traceability, data interoperability, sustainable financing mechanisms, and inclusive business partnerships, with targeted sessions on integrating traceability systems for key regional commodities (coffee, cocoa, palm oil) and strengthening multi-stakeholder cooperation. Through workshops, dialogues, and technical exchanges, participants gained actionable insights to strengthen EUDR compliance capacity, foster interoperable data governance, and catalyze inclusive supply-chain transformation with a focus on smallholders and exporting actors. This capacity-sharing platform also fostered cross-sectoral networking and aligned institutional partners on next steps for collaborative implementation of traceability and compliance instruments in the region.

The article aims to strengthen policy discourse around sustainable farming practices that help farmers adapt to climate change impacts. By reaching a broad readership through this prominent media platform, IRRI contributes to building public understanding and support for climate-smart agriculture policies in Bangladesh, where climate change poses significant challenges to food security and rural livelihoods.

results.title: Presented at American Geophysical Union Annual Meeting (AGU25):A Cloud-Based Google Earth Engine (GEE) Approach for Irrigation Demand Forecasting Using Multi-Sensor Satellite and Machine Learning Techniques
results.description: IWMI researchers presented a new cloud-based irrigation forecasting system at the American Geophysical Union Annual Meeting, addressing the critical gap in predicting irrigation water demand. The system operates within Google Earth Engine and integrates with Google Colab platform, using multiple satellite sensors and machine learning techniques to analyze geospatial remote sensing data. This innovation enables early irrigation forecasting to help farmers and water managers better plan water use, particularly important for climate adaptation and food security. The presentation shared this technological advancement with the global scientific community, demonstrating how satellite technology and artificial intelligence can support more efficient agricultural water management worldwide.

results.title: PhD training on drought experiments with yam varieties
results.description: PhD student; Mansurat, received specialized training on conducting drought experiments with yam varieties at the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) in Ibadan, Nigeria. The training focused on understanding the biological mechanisms that help yam plants survive drought conditions. CGIAR's Breeding for Tomorrow initiative provided technical support for establishing field trials and experimental design. This capacity building effort aims to strengthen local research capabilities for developing climate-resilient yam varieties that can better withstand water stress, ultimately benefiting smallholder farmers who depend on yam cultivation in drought-prone regions of West Africa.

results.title: Farmer seed producer associations in Tanzania demonstrate organizational benefits from modernized cassava and sweet potato seed systems
results.description: Farmer Seed Producers Assocations have been established through CGIAR coordinated seed system interventions aimed at improving the commercial viability and sustainability of seed systems for vegetatively propagated crops (VPCs). Two of these associations are based in the north-western Lake Zone of Tanzania. One of them focuses on cassava while the other works with sweet potato. The associations have expanded the range of support functions that they provide. As well as helping member seed producers access certified seed, and market the seed that they produce, the associations increasingly support members with small loan schemes, coordinate engagement with regulatory authorities (for seed inspection) and provide a group focal point through which large customers, such as government offices or NGOs can interact in a professional manner. The success of the associations is confirmed by a steady growth in the number of members. Given these achievements, a video was produced in 2025 with the aim of communicating these successes. Two versions of this were published on the IITA Youtube channel. The original video is in Swahili, but has English sub-titles. A second version has a Yoruba voice-over. In 2026, the video will be shared with VPC seed producers in south-western with the aim of stimulating the development and/or strengthening of similar associations in Nigeria. Further dissemination will be achieved by adding this content to the seed system toolkits available or being developed for the TAAT e-catalog.

results.title: Water Impact Calculator: A decision support tool for irrigation scheduling
results.description: The Water Impact Calculator (WIC) is a decision-support tool designed to promote need-based and efficient irrigation management in agriculture. Unlike conventional practices that rely on fixed schedules or farmer intuition, WIC uses a field water budget approach to align irrigation with actual crop water requirements. By integrating basic field information such as soil type, land slope, sowing date, and crop duration with real-time weather and rainfall data, the tool estimates evapotranspiration and crop water demand accurately. WIC continuously tracks the soil water balance in the root zone and generates timely irrigation alerts when moisture levels fall below critical thresholds. A key feature of the tool is its adaptive feedback mechanism, which recalibrates future irrigation recommendations based on actual water application. Importantly, WIC offers a cost-effective alternative to sensor-based systems, making precision irrigation accessible to small and marginal farmers. By reducing water wastage, energy use, and crop stress, the tool enhances water use efficiency, improves crop productivity, and supports climate-resilient agricultural practices.

results.title: Detection of pesticide and antibiotic residues in vegetable crops
results.description: Pesticide and antibiotic residues were detected and quantified in vegetable crops from Ghana, Benin, and Cameroon. A minimum of 30 samples per country were analyzed using High Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) screening. Nine pesticides were targeted: Emamectin benzoate, Acetamiprid, Chlorfenapyr, Lambda-cyhalothrin, Chlorpyrifos, Cypermethrin, Deltamethrin, Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT), and Permethrin. Five antibiotics were tested: Amoxicillin, Ciprofloxacin, Metronidazole, Penicillin G, and Gentamicin. All analyzed samples contained residues of at least one pesticide, with Emamectin benzoate, Chlorfenapyr, Lambda-cyhalothrin, and Chlorpyrifos being most frequently detected. Antibiotic residues were detected in samples from Benin, specifically in Ocimum gratissimum, with traces of Ciprofloxacin, Penicillin G, and Gentamicin. Analyses for Cameroon and additional samples from Ghana and Benin are ongoing. The presence of these residues likely results from the misuse or overuse of pesticides and antibiotics in vegetable production, though plants may also synthesize some compounds naturally as defense mechanisms. Residue accumulation poses potential risks to human nutrition and health. Ongoing investigations aim to identify additional residues, sources of contamination, and the possible role of plant-synthesized protective compounds, providing essential information for ensuring vegetable safety before consumption.

results.title: Postgraduate course “Research in practice - Seed systems of opportunity crops and the diversification of food systems” (23 March – 3 April 2025, Uganda)
results.description:
This intensive postgraduate training on seed systems of so-called Neglected and Underutilized Species (NUS) was co-organized by Wageningen University, CIP, The Alliance, NORAD and Oxfam-NOVIB. It targeted PhD students, postdocs and practitioners. A total of 30 participants from over 10 countries – including Peru, Tanzania, Uganda, Malawi and Nepal - received a 2-week intense training on the diverse aspects of NUS Seed Systems. The training was rated outstanding by participants in the final evaluation.    

The goal of this course was to co-develop knowledge among practitioners and researchers to increase the value and role of NUS in seed- and food- systems. This course followed and built on the earlier postgraduate course 'Participatory Plant Breeding and Resilient Seed Systems' (2022) and ‘Smallholder Engagement in Seed Systems’ (2023). The course was held from 23 March – 3 April 2025. The start and finish was at Makerere University Agricultural Research Institute Kabanyolo (MUARIK), Uganda (near Kampala). Field sites are approximately 30 min away from Mbarara and Soroti, the cities where participants will stay during the practice-oriented week of field work.

results.title: CGIAR and FAO joint submission advocates for food systems inclusion in global climate transition policies
results.description: CGIAR collaborated with the Food and Agriculture Organization to submit a comprehensive policy document to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change's fourth Just Transition Work Programme dialogue. This submission emphasized that equitable climate transitions cannot succeed without transforming food systems and supporting smallholder farmers. The document provided concrete solutions and opportunities for integrating agricultural considerations into climate policy. As a result of this advocacy effort, the final programme text now explicitly recognizes the need for whole-of-economy approaches that engage rural actors, especially smallholder farmers, in creating sustainable livelihoods while maintaining food production during climate transitions.

results.title: Completion of Masters degree with thesis on the the effect of governance on production efficiency in coastal Banagladesh, insights from rice farmers with assistance from IRRI
results.description: A MS female student was able to graduate with technical assistance from IRRI. Her MS thesis examines the effect of governance on rice production efficiency in coastal Bangladesh, using farm-level data to analyze how institutional quality, service delivery, and regulatory effectiveness shape farmers’ technical efficiency. The study provides empirical evidence on the role of governance mechanisms in mediating productivity outcomes under climate stress, offering policy-relevant insights for strengthening enabling environments in coastal rice systems. Aligned with the **Scaling for Impact Initiative**, the findings inform pathways for translating governance reforms into measurable efficiency gains and resilient agricultural development.

results.title: IRRI shares community-based climate adaptation approaches at COP30 global climate conference in Brazil
results.description: At COP30 in Belém, Brazil (November 2025), global climate action shifted decisively from commitments to implementation, with Locally Led Adaptation (LLA) at the center. IRRI, represented by Dr. Jon Hellin, across four dialogues, demonstrating how science can operationalize LLA to strengthen community agency, equity, and finance. Key discussions emphasized “business unusual” research, showcasing Living Labs, positive deviance, and community-based adaptation planning as practical pathways for transformative adaptation. IRRI highlighted its role in providing analytical rigor, system thinking, and partnership brokering with institutions such as the World Bank and Gates Foundation. Sessions also stressed equitable adaptation finance, closing data gaps, and integrating mitigation–adaptation solutions. A strong focus on gender and youth underscored the urgency of investing in women farmers and young innovators as leaders of resilient, locally grounded food systems.

results.title: High-level climate security dialogue organized for Middle East and North Africa stakeholders by CGIAR
results.description: The Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT organized a high-level capacity sharing session at the 4th Montreal Climate Security Summit, bringing together 100 participants to address climate security challenges in the Middle East and North Africa region. This focused dialogue examined the interconnections between climate change and security risks, exploring how environmental degradation and climate impacts threaten stability in the region. Participants discussed evidence-based policy and programmatic solutions to strengthen resilience and reduce climate-related security vulnerabilities. The session facilitated knowledge exchange among researchers, policymakers, and practitioners, contributing to enhanced understanding of climate security dynamics and potential response strategies for one of the world's most climate-vulnerable regions.

results.title: Awareness-raising events for the primary school students and teachers on nutritional benefits of small fish and small fish powder to improve children’s nutrition and support school feeding practices in Cambodia
results.description: To improve children’s nutrition and support school feeding practices, WorldFish through CGIAR Scaling for Impact Program (S4I) in collaboration with International Institute of Rural Reconstruction (IIRR) initiated awareness-raising activities on the production and use of small fish powder. This initiative responds to the need for affordable, nutrient-rich food options that can be easily prepared at home and integrated into daily meals for school children. During the reporting period, the project organized 28 awareness-raising sessions in target primary schools. Across all sessions, a total of 1,251 participants, including 671 females and girls attended the events. The participants also included school teacher representatives and students. The sessions aimed to: (1) introduce the nutritional benefits of small fish powder for children, (2) demonstrate simple household techniques for processing and preserving small fish; and (3) increase family-level adoption of nutritious, locally available foods.

results.title: Soils of ILRI’s Kapiti Research Station and Wildlife Conservancy
results.description: The soil survey report of the International Livestock Research Institute’s (ILRI) Kapiti Research Station and Wildlife Conservancy is the first of its kind. Previous work on the distribution of soils in the survey area is limited to the 1:1,000,000 Exploratory Soil Map of Kenya prepared by the Kenya Soil Survey (KSS) and the soils are described in very general terms. The current report is more detailed and serves as an important explanatory note to the soil conditions of ILRI’s ranch. The accompanying soil map covers an area of 13,000 hectares (ha). The study area falls in Agro-Climatic Zone IV which is semiarid. The site experiences a bimodal rainfall distribution with long rains from mid-March to May and short rains from mid-October to December. The mean annual total rainfall is 552 ± 203 mm. The area is underlain by Archaean Basement system rocks, Tertiary volcanic rocks (mainly composed of Kapiti Phonolites), and Pleistocene and Quaternary sediments. The topography of the area is dominated by very gently undulating plains interrupted, in the middle of the survey area, by hills with their associated foot slopes.

results.title: AKILIMO Tanzania PAASS Platform for Institutional Strengthening, Sustainable Financing, Digital Advisory Expansion, and Coordinated Scaling within National Partnership Frameworks
results.description:
The AKILIMO Tanzania Association (ATA) convenes member organizations and strategic partners to review performance, set priorities, and guide the continued delivery of AKILIMO services as national ownership increases beyond donor-funded projects. ATA operates as a credible, accountable platform for coordinating digital advisory scaling in Tanzania.

AKILIMO functions as an integrated, partner-driven decision-support system that uses system analysis tools to translate agronomic evidence, digital data, and extension approaches into practical recommendations. Delivered through multiple formats, the system links tailored guidance with training and extension workflows, supporting farmer uptake and improved income outcomes through coordinated deployment.

Through structured discussions, partners identified key priorities: strengthening governance, developing a sustainable business model, expanding coverage to additional crops, enhancing interoperability with other advisory platforms, and clarifying ATA’s positioning within the SFP and PAASS framework.

results.title: From evidence to action: Spatial diversification boosts productivity but cannot overcome climate-driven yield decline without customized integration of soil and management strategies.
results.description: Nationwide 10-km simulation modeling identifies maize-legume rotations as a superior strategy for productivity and stability, cutting yield risk and increasing maize-equivalent yields. However, even these optimized systems show a persistent -120 kg ha⁻¹ decade⁻¹ yield trend, signaling an urgent climate threat to Malawi's food base. Our analysis provides the first high-resolution, long-term evidence that diversification alone is insufficient. The findings mandate a policy shift toward integrated packages that combine spatial targeting of rotations with investments in soil fertility and adaptive management to secure long-term food production.

results.title: Workshop for researchers, farmers, government and private sector stakeholders in Makueni County, Kenya, to learn strategies for scaling sustainable agricultural practices
results.description: This workshop brought together 50+ participants from research institutions, government agencies, private sector companies, and farmer organizations in Makueni County, Kenya, to learn strategies for scaling sustainable agricultural practices. Organized by CGIAR's Scaling for Impact Science Program with partner programs, the event built on conservation agriculture work from the Ukama Ustawi Initiative across three Kenyan counties. Participants shared experiences and discussed integrated approaches combining technological innovations, social strategies, and financial models. Key learning outcomes included the importance of context-specific solutions, participatory methods, digital advisory tools, and multi-stakeholder partnerships for achieving sustainable scale in agrifood systems.

results.title: Demand-led seed systems linking traders, producers and farmers increase improved bean variety adoption across seven African countries
results.description: Seven African countries—Cameroon, Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe—have successfully implemented trader-centered seed system models that connect seed producers directly with farmers through market-driven mechanisms. Developed under CGIAR's Breeding for Tomorrow initiative with Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT support, these innovative approaches have increased adoption of improved bean varieties by placing traders at the center of seed distribution networks. Each country adapted the model to local contexts: Zambia and Rwanda established Multi-Stakeholder Platforms with trader leadership, while Uganda and Ethiopia integrated digital tools and export contracts to strengthen market linkages. Key innovations include trader-financed seed production, digital tracking systems, and participatory variety selection that responds to actual market demand rather than supply-driven approaches, demonstrating how market mechanisms can transform traditional seed systems across diverse African agricultural contexts.

results.title: Agricultural mechanization in Honduras: characterization, challenges, and opportunities for maize, beans, and coffee production systems
results.description: CIMMYT and Universidad Zamorano carried out a study across five departments of Honduras (Lempira, Copán, Intibucá, Olancho, and El Paraíso) to characterize farmers’ use of tools and machinery in maize, bean, and coffee systems, and to identify key challenges and opportunities for mechanization. In total, 112 structured surveys of farmers were conducted. This dataset includes the survey results, providing information about household and farm characteristics, crops grown and area per crop, plot location and topography (hillsides, plains, or mixed terrain), and the tools and machinery used in each operation, such as land preparation, planting, weeding, harvesting, and post-harvest. It also includes information about access to mechanization services, reasons for lacking machinery, perceived benefits of using machinery, and cropping cycle stages that need mechanization, among other details. This can help guide the design of mechanization pathways suited to smallholder conditions in Honduras.

results.title: Low Trophic Aquaculture Screening Framework: a digital analytical framework to assess low trophic aquatic species for sustainable aquaculture decision-making
results.description: Reliable decisions on aquaculture development are often constrained by limited and uneven information on many fish species, particularly those feeding low in the food chain and with potential for sustainable production. The Low Trophic Aquaculture Screening Framework is designed to structure and interpret available evidence on locally occurring fish species in a transparent and systematic way. The framework organizes existing biological, nutritional, and production-related information into a small set of comparative indicators that allow species to be screened and compared, even when detailed data are not available. It draws on widely used global information sources, such as FishBase, and complements them with insights from published research and practitioner experience, explicitly documenting uncertainties and data gaps rather than masking them.  As an initial test, the framework was applied to freshwater and brackish water species that are native or commonly present in specific regions, using a limited number of parameters to explore relationships between feeding level, growth characteristics, nutritional value, and current use in aquaculture. The exploratory analysis demonstrated that meaningful patterns can be identified using partial data, while also highlighting where additional information is needed to improve confidence and relevance. By providing a structured way to compare locally relevant species under data-limited conditions, the Low Trophic Aquaculture Screening Framework supports research prioritization, helps identify low trophic species with potential for sustainable aquaculture development, and guides future data collection efforts. It lays the groundwork for more advanced analytical and decision-support tools and contributes to data-driven approaches that can inform aquaculture planning, policy discussions, and investment choices as evidence and capacity grow.

results.title: Quezon City government institutionalizes vendor business school program to support informal food vendors across the Philippines
results.description: The Local Government of Quezon City has officially adopted and scaled up a pilot vendor business school program, transforming it from a research initiative into citywide policy. This institutionalization empowers informal food vendors who serve urban communities daily by providing them with business skills and support. The policy change represents successful collaboration between CGIAR research centers (CIP, ILRI, and IRRI) and local government, demonstrating how research can drive practical policy solutions. The program addresses the needs of vulnerable informal sector workers, particularly women, while strengthening urban food systems. This policy adoption serves as a model for other cities seeking to support informal food vendors and improve urban food security.

results.title: Strengthening nutrition, health, and food security in Nigeria: policy and programming alignment for innovation scaling
results.description:
Nigeria faces a deepening crisis in nutrition, health and food security, driven by high levels of malnutrition, climate vulnerability, poverty, and weak institutional systems. Despite having an extensive set of national policies and programs such as the National Multi-Sectoral Plan of Action for Food and Nutrition (NMPFAN), the Agricultural Sector Food Security and Nutrition Strategy (AFSNS), and the National Agricultural Technology and Innovation Policy (NATIP), implementation remains weak. The report reviews 23 policies and 24 institutional programs, revealing strong aspirational commitments but limited actionable demand. Only a fraction of policies include clear budgets, coordinated implementation plans, or mechanisms for scaling innovations. 

Key gaps include fragmented governance, inadequate financing, weak monitoring and evaluation systems, and insufficient focus on sub-national realities. Agriculture and health budgets fall far below continental commitments, contributing to low program effectiveness. Many innovations such as biofortified crops, digital agriculture solutions, and climate-smart technologies, exist but remain under-scaled due to poor institutional readiness. 

The report concludes that CGIAR’s Scaling for Impact (S4I) program is well positioned to bridge the gap between policy intent and practical implementation by supporting evidence-based decision-making, strengthening institutional capacity, improving data systems, and co-designing bundled innovations with government, donors, and private sector partners to achieve sustainable, large-scale impact across Nigeria’s agrifood systems.

results.title: Enhanced digital platform delivering localized climate advisories (EDACaP) upgraded by CIMMYT and Alliance researchers for Ethiopian smallholder farmers
results.description: Climate variability poses significant challenges for smallholder farmers who lack access to timely, relevant weather information for agricultural decision-making. CIMMYT and Alliance researchers enhanced the existing Digital AgroClimate Advisory Platform (EDACaP) to better serve Ethiopian farmers with improved functionality and user experience. The upgraded platform transforms complex climate data into practical farming guidance, helping users understand when to plant, irrigate, or harvest based on local weather patterns. Interactive features allow farmers to provide feedback and access learning materials tailored to their specific conditions. This enhancement builds on previous climate information systems to create a more responsive tool that supports agricultural resilience and productivity in variable climate conditions.

results.title: Training session on Common Bean Observatory platform delivered to bean breeding researchers by Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT
results.description:
The Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT delivered training to bean breeding researchers on the Common Bean Observatory, an open-access digital platform that consolidates data on production, consumption, trade, varietal releases, and seed systems for common beans.

During the session, researchers are introduced to the Observatory as a centralized, open-access platform that brings together data on production, consumption, trade, varietal release, seed systems, and policy environments for common bean. The presentation emphasizes how the tool consolidates information from multiple national and international sources into a coherent set of indicators that can be explored through interactive dashboards and visualizations. This integrated view enables breeding teams to move beyond isolated datasets and better understand the broader contexts in which improved varieties are developed, disseminated, and adopted.

A key focus of the event is demonstrating the relevance of the Observatory to breeding programs. The tool is presented as a resource for aligning breeding priorities with real-world demand, identifying geographic and socio-economic patterns that influence adoption, and tracking progress toward development outcomes. By situating breeding outputs within market trends, production systems, and food security indicators, the Observatory supports researchers in framing breeding objectives that are responsive to farmers’, consumers’, and value-chain needs.

The presentation also highlights opportunities for engagement, encouraging researchers to use the Observatory not only as an information source but as a learning and collaboration platform. Feedback from breeding teams is positioned as essential for refining indicators, improving data relevance, and ensuring the tool evolves alongside research priorities. Overall, the event serves to bridge data science and plant breeding, reinforcing the role of shared, accessible evidence in accelerating impact from common bean research.

results.title: Cambodia's Ministry of Agriculture adopts national program scaling climate-resilient rice innovations developed by IRRI and partners
results.description: Cambodia's Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry (MAFF) and Ministry of Environment (MOE) launched the 'Promoting Climate Resilient Landscapes in the Tonle Sap' national program to scale up climate-resilient rice production innovations. These innovations were originally developed and tested through CGIAR initiatives led by the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) and partners in Cambodia. The program addresses the urgent need to help rice farmers adapt to climate change impacts in the Tonle Sap region, one of Cambodia's most important agricultural areas. By adopting these proven innovations at the national level, the government aims to strengthen food security and farmer livelihoods while building resilience against climate variability and extreme weather events affecting rice production systems.

results.title: From Research to Markets: Presenting Global Market Intelligence Tools to EMBRAPA to Understand Cassava Value Chains
results.description:
The presentation “From Research to Markets: Global Perspectives from Cassava” was delivered as part of the EMBRAPA webinar series Desde la investigación hacia los mercados: Perspectivas globales de la yuca, a live broadcast aimed at strengthening dialogue between research and market-oriented decision making in cassava. The session brought together approximately 61 participants connected live, including members of the socioeconomic agriculture network and researchers from Embrapa, to discuss current trends, challenges, and opportunities in cassava markets at both regional and global scales.

The presentation focused on showcasing data-driven tools developed to support market intelligence and strategic planning for cassava. Particular emphasis was placed on the Crop Observatories and the Global Market Intelligence Platform (GloMIP), which were introduced as complementary resources for exploring production, demand, market segmentation, and breeding pipelines. A dedicated slide included a QR code linking directly to these platforms, encouraging participants to further explore the tools and engage with the underlying data beyond the webinar. Through live explanations and examples, the presentation illustrated how these tools can support evidence-based decisions, including projections on productivity and insights into evolving market segments.

The presentation was delivered between minute 7:30 and 30:12 of the broadcast, which is publicly available on YouTube. To date, the video has accumulated over 1,000 views, reflecting a solid level of engagement given the technical and scientific nature of the content. The event provided a valuable opportunity to connect with Brazil—a major global producer of cassava and a key partner in collaborative research—and to position market intelligence tools as practical bridges between agricultural research and market outcomes.

results.title: Digital soil sensing technology tested by ICRISAT to rapidly assess soil properties for farmers in India
results.description:
This probe explores the use of novel digital sensing and data-driven approaches to rapidly assess soil properties and support future decision-making in agriculture. Traditional soil testing methods are often slow, costly, and difficult to scale across large farming landscapes, limiting their usefulness for timely farm management and policy planning. This probe examines an alternative approach that treats soil assessment as an information system rather than a laboratory procedure.

The probe focuses on the use of portable field-based sensing tools that capture how light interacts with soil. These soil signatures are analyzed using advanced data-processing methods to estimate key soil characteristics without the need for chemical reagents. By combining field measurements with digital modeling techniques, the probe investigates how soil information can be generated quickly, at lower cost, and across wider spatial scales.

Rather than delivering an operational service, the probe is designed to test and understand the potential system-level implications of this frontier digital approach. It examines questions related to scalability, data quality, model reliability, and how such technologies could transform future soil health assessment, fertilizer management, and land-use decision-making.

The probe contributes evidence on how emerging digital sensing and analytical technologies could reshape soil diagnostics, inform sustainable resource management, and support future agricultural decision systems. Insights from this work are intended to guide researchers, program designers, and decision-makers in evaluating the opportunities, limitations, and governance considerations of adopting next-generation digital soil assessment technologies at scale.

results.title: Institutional demand and supply for capacity sharing mapped to guide the design of the CapSha Marketplace
results.description:
In 2025, CapSha completed an initial mapping of institutional capacity sharing demand, supply, and constraints across CGIAR and partner organizations through a structured survey and preliminary analysis. The mapping was implemented during CGIAR Science Week (April 2025) and generated 29 individual responses from 16 countries, spanning Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, and South America.

The preliminary analysis produced clear demand signals on what institutions prioritize for strengthening capacity, including strong interest in technical and scientific skills, as well as growing importance of digital skills and shared online knowledge platforms. The results also documented the types of capacity development services and expertise institutions currently provide, such as training and mentorship programs, partnerships and networks, access to data and evidence, and use of online resources.

In addition, the mapping identified major constraints affecting both access to and provision of capacity sharing opportunities, with financial resources, institutional capacity limitations, and partner-finding challenges emerging prominently. Respondents also provided practical suggestions on how CapSha could improve support, including expanding exchange opportunities, strengthening partnerships, and improving access to shared resources.

Overall, this output provided an evidence base to orient and prioritize CapSha’s actions and to inform the user-focused design of the global Capacity Sharing Marketplace.

results.title: Current Practices and Production in Ricefield Pond Systems around Boeng Sneh, Prey Veng, Cambodia’s Multifunctional Landscapes
results.description: Rice-field pond (RFP) systems have become vital micro-reservoirs within Cambodia’s rice-based farming landscapes, offering multifunctional benefits for water security, fish, and household nutrition. This study investigates RFP practices around Boeng Sneh in Prey Veng Province, based on structured interviews with 121 households across eight communes. Findings reveal that rice cultivation remains the dominant livelihood, yet RFPs contribute significantly to diversification, providing average fish yields of 51 kg per year from ponds of 250 m², with incomes nearly seven times higher per unit area than rice. That practice found more than 20 years ago, driven by food security programs and mechanized excavation, but management practices remain unbalanced.

results.title: Findings from Integrated Rice-Field Pond Systems
results.description: At the inter-provincial workshop in Prey Veng, organized by the Council for Agricultural and Rural Development (CARD) under the CGIAR S4I, SAAF, and MFL programs, stakeholders from government, community, and development partners gathered to strengthen district-level food system governance. The presentation on Integrated Rice-Field Pond (RFP) systems highlighted their importance in Cambodia’s rice-growing regions, where one in three households maintain ponds that provide fish harvests averaging 40 kilograms per year. These ponds serve as refuges for fish during dry seasons and pesticide exposure, while also supporting diversified livelihoods. Findings from studies around Boeng Sneh revealed that rice farming remains the dominant livelihood, but RFP systems contribute significantly to household food and income security. Despite challenges such as pond drying, pesticide use, and unsustainable fishing practices, good management approaches; like aquatic plant cultivation, fish shelters, and broodstock retention; demonstrated potential for resilience and productivity.

results.title: IFPRI Welfare-Assessment Method Integrating Learning, Lifetime Earnings, and Equity to Guide School Feeding Investments in Fragile Settings
results.description:
This innovation is a replicable analytical method developed by the International Food Policy Research Institute to evaluate school feeding and similar programs that build human capital.
The approach combines evidence from randomized trials on learning and nutrition outcomes with projections of lifetime earnings and models distributional effects across population groups, allowing decision-makers to assess overall social returns in a single, transparent benefit–cost framework.
Previously, economic evaluations of school feeding often considered short-term outcomes or financial returns alone. This method addresses that gap by explicitly valuing education gains, long-term income impacts, and equity benefits for disadvantaged children, making it suitable for humanitarian and development contexts where trade-offs across objectives are acute.
The innovation was developed through IFPRI-led research synthesized in a global review of school-meal evidence and formalized through a peer-reviewed application demonstrating the method for national school feeding programs. It is designed for adaptation by governments, donors, and humanitarian agencies seeking to prioritize investments that improve nutrition, learning, and resilience in fragile environments

LKP is designed for use by extension workers, crop advisors, input providers, and providers of services who interview a farmer using a computer or smartphone. Each guideline provides an actionable recommendation, which matches the locationspecific cropping practices and needs of a farmer."

results.title: Consolidating gender mainstreaming in national climate policy: Lessons and recommendations for NDCs and the National Climate Change Action Plan (NAPCC)
results.description:
This policy brief analyzes the integration of gender equality and social inclusion within Guatemala’s climate policy framework, with the aim of providing technical evidence to inform the updating of the Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and the National Climate Change Action Plan (PANCC). The analysis draws on a review of the literature, institutional interviews, and a systematic assessment of the 22 Departmental Climate Change Adaptation Plans (PDACC), conducted by means of a standardized Excel-based analysis matrix. The qualitative and comparative evaluation of adaptation measures was based on a contextualized GESI framework, grounded in the gender-responsive adaptation dimensions proposed by Dazé and Dekens (2017) and operationalized through the Reach–Benefit–Empower–Transform (RBET) framework developed by Crossland et al. (2022), enabling the classification of actions according to their level of inclusiveness.

The findings reveal significant gaps between national commitments and their implementation at the territorial level. Although 19 of the 22 PDACC explicitly reference a gender approach, most adaptation measures lack clear operational strategies, defined implementation mechanisms, and sex-disaggregated indicators or other relevant social variables. This situation limits the effective translation of gender equality and social inclusion into climate action at the departmental level. The resulting database constitutes a technical input to strengthen territorial planning and support the updating processes of the PANCC and the NDC, highlighting the Gender and Climate Change Action Plan (PAGcc) as a key tool for advancing more inclusive, coherent, and territorially grounded climate action.

Este policy brief analiza la incorporación del enfoque de género y de inclusión social en la política climática de Guatemala, con el propósito de aportar evidencia técnica para la actualización de la Contribución Determinada a Nivel Nacional (NDC) y del Plan Nacional de Acción Climática (PANCC). El análisis se sustenta en la revisión de literatura, entrevistas institucionales y una evaluación sistemática de los 22 Planes Departamentales de Adaptación al Cambio Climático (PDACC), realizada por medio de una matriz de análisis estandarizada en formato Excel. La evaluación cualitativa y comparativa de las medidas de adaptación se basó en un marco GESI contextualizado, fundamentado en las dimensiones de adaptación con enfoque de género propuestas por Dazé y Dekens (2017) y operacionalizado a través del marco Reach–Benefit–Empower–Transform (RBET) de Crossland et al. (2022), lo que permitió clasificar las acciones según su nivel de inclusividad.

Los resultados evidencian brechas relevantes entre los compromisos nacionales y su implementación a nivel territorial. Aunque 19 de los 22 PDACC hacen referencia explícita al enfoque de género, la mayoría de las medidas de adaptación carecen de estrategias operativas claras, mecanismos de implementación definidos e indicadores desagregados por sexo u otras variables sociales relevantes. Esta situación limita la traducción efectiva del enfoque de género y de inclusión social en la acción climática a nivel departamental. La base de datos generada constituye un insumo técnico para fortalecer la planificación territorial y apoyar los procesos de actualización del PANCC y la NDC, destacando el Plan de Acción de Género y Cambio Climático (PAGcc) como una herramienta clave para avanzar hacia una acción climática más inclusiva, coherente y territorialmente anclada.

results.title: Gender issues and gaps in school meal programs research: A scoping review protocol
results.description: This scoping review protocol maps out the process for a forthcoming scoping study on gender issues in school meals programs. Due to their large and multi-sectoral reach, school meal programs have the potential to drive progress toward gender equality on a global scale, or alternatively, to perpetuate inequality. Gender considerations related to school meal programs pertain to issues such as: food and nutrition security; school enrolment, attendance, and educational achievement; agrifood systems and agricultural production; and rural economies and livelihoods, to name a few. A robust evidence base on gender in school meal programs is needed to inform the design and delivery of gender-sensitive programs. This scoping review is intended to provide a critical first step to understanding the current research landscape to inform future research pathways. More holistic and nuanced gender research can be used as a critical evidence base to inform more inclusive, effective, and fair school meal programs for all.

results.title: Participatory field testing of the redesigned Farmer Feedback Sheet & Diploma for feedback after tricot trials
results.description: As part of the 1000FARMS Platform project, this webinar shared findings from a field test of redesigned feedback tools developed to support participatory variety trials in Nigeria. The session focused on a new version of the Farmer Feedback Sheet and diploma, tested with cassava farmers and trial facilitators in south-west Nigeria. By applying human-centered design methods, the team assessed the usability and relevance of the tools and explored their role in enhancing communication between farmers and implementers. The results informed practical design improvements and facilitation strategies to help partners conduct more inclusive and engaging farmer feedback sessions at scale. The presenters: Juan Manuel Londoño is a UX designer dedicated to transforming research findings into practical digital and analog tools for smallholder farmers. He has been involved in product design and field-testing activities in Colombia, Guatemala, and Honduras. Anna Müller heads the Human-Centered and Inclusive Design team at the Alliance. With a PhD in Agricultural Economics and field experience in Central America and East Africa, she guides projects that apply user-research methods to digital extension, breeding, and on-farm testing services.

results.title: Empowering Agriculture through Agro-Climate Advisory Services in Ethiopia: Agro-climate advisory for Training of Trainers (ToT)
results.description: This training manual focuses on Training of Trainers (ToT). It aims to equip them with the basic knowledge, skills, and communication channels framework required to disseminate effective agro-climate advisory (AgCA) services to smallholder farmers. The manual begins with the definitions and descriptions of AgCA, followed by the purpose, key objectives, and other essential components. It covers the basics of climate, including weather, climate variability, and climate change, as well as their impact on agricultural productivity. Recognizing the importance of establishing the value chain of partners and farming communities, the manual highlights participatory approaches and integrating local knowledge into actionable AgCA services in a comprehensive end-to-end manner.

results.title: Tracking a decade of food system transformation in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta: production, consumption, and nutrition
results.description: Global deltas, including Vietnam’s Mekong River Delta (MRD), are fertile, densely populated, and vital for food production, yet their low-lying terrain leaves them highly vulnerable to climate change. By utilizing national data from the Vietnam Household Living Standards Surveys (VHLSS), Statistical Year Books (SYB), and General Nutrition Surveys (GNS), this study examines the changes in food production, consumption patterns, diet, and nutrition in the region from 2010 to 2020. The MRD remains the largest food production region in the country across all food groups, with output far exceeding local nutrient needs, yet paradoxically exhibits the second lowest dietary diversity nationally. Agricultural production has shifted from staples toward fruit and aquatic products, but a critical production-consumption disconnect driven by market orientation has led diets toward more animal-source foods, sugar-sweetened products, and food away from home (FAFH). While nutrient adequacy improved in energy, protein, and retinol, it declined in calcium, and household consumption of self-produced food dropped dramatically across all food groups. The dietary transition contributed to substantial improvements in child nutrition status in all forms, with stunting rates decreasing by nearly 16%, underweight by 10%, and wasting by 4%. However, it also led to the highest increases in overweight and obesity rates nationally, rising threefold among children aged 6-19 years (23.8%) and adults (34% for both men and women), with sugar-sweetened beverage consumption increasing fourfold. This production-consumption paradox in which agricultural abundance coexists with poor dietary quality, demonstrates the limitations of production-focused policies and underscores the urgent need for integrated food system approaches that align production with sustainable, healthy diets under the pressures of climate change and urbanization.

results.title: Developing approaches for more socially inclusive climate-smart livestock practices
results.description: Gender and social inclusion were mainstreamed across all work packages within the CGIAR Research Initiative on Livestock and Climate. The focus within Work Packages 1 and 3 was on household and systems-level research. Researchers generated evidence to address critical research gaps in understanding how intra-household and community-wide social dynamics impact and interact with adaptation capacities that bolster resilience by working with communities and partners in priority sites in Kenya, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Tunisia and Colombia. Initiative gender researchers and interdisciplinary teams and partners then identified and co-designed gender accommodative and transformative approaches to support socially inclusive adaptation and resilient communities and landscapes. Evidence across work packages informed the development of tailored approaches that were piloted to address specific needs, access to resources and adaptive capacities. Two primary pathways were identified to 1) collate evidence and research gaps and 2) implement and scale approaches for socially inclusive adaptation.

results.title: What is the nature of the evidence base on climate variability and extreme weather impacts on diets and nutritional status among marginalized agri-food system workers and micro, small- and medium-sized enterprises in low- and middle- income countries? : A Protocol for Systematic Evidence and Gap Map
results.description:
While evidence linking climate change to a range of nutrition outcomes is growing, existing reviews are often narrow in scope, geographically limited, or focused on broad vulnerable populations rather than marginalized food system workers and MSMEs specifically. No review to date synthesizes climate-related food and nutrition security impacts on marginalized agri-food system workers and MSMEs with an explicit focus on gender and Indigenous communities. Understanding how climate change affects the diets and nutrition of these groups is critical for building equitable, effective climate adaptation and food system transformation strategies. Women and Indigenous Peoples are not only more exposed to climate-related shocks, but also often hold key knowledge systems and play central roles in household food security and ecosystem stewardship. Overlooking their specific vulnerabilities, capacities, and constraints risks reinforcing inequality and undermining resilience.
Therefore, this systematic map aims to fill this knowledge gap by centering these communities –marginalized food system workers and MSMEs – providing an evidence base for equity-focused interventions and ensuring that the needs and voices of those most affected by climate change are reflected in global and national response.

results.title: Stocktaking of policy, institutional readiness, and carbon initiatives for Just Low-carbon Transitions in the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam
results.description: This synthesis report consolidates the information on the policy landscape, institutional readiness, and carbon-mitigation initiatives in the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam, with a specific focus on accelerating methane reductions in rice systems. It reviews national climate commitments (NDCs), sectoral policies, and regulatory frameworks influencing low-carbon rice cultivation, particularly the adoption of AWD and related climate-smart practices. The report also provides detailed assessments of each country’s carbon market initiatives—including CDM, voluntary carbon market projects, Article 6 readiness, results-based climate finance, and emerging JCM projects—and evaluates institutional capacity for monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV). Through comparative stakeholder mapping and synthesis tables, the publication identifies gaps, opportunities, and practical entry points for promoting just and inclusive low-carbon transitions across major rice-producing economies in Southeast Asia

results.title: Scaling Fund Report 2025
results.description: The CGIAR Scaling Fund is a strategic financing and technical support mechanism designed to bridge the gap between innovation development and impact at scale by combining flexible funding with tailored, hands-on scaling support. Anchored in CGIAR’s commitment to responsible and demand-driven scaling, the Fund supports innovation teams to translate research outputs into context-specific solutions with measurable benefits, while anticipating and mitigating social and environmental risks. In 2025, the Fund supported eight innovation teams across six CGIAR science programs, five CGIAR centers, and 11 countries through a dual structure comprising the competitive Scaling Challenge and the flexible Needs-Driven Support window, complemented by a strategic partnership with ENABEL. Now in its third year, the Scaling Fund continues to embed scaling science into practice, strengthen partnerships, and advance equitable, sustainable impact at scale.

results.title: Capacity building and training: Technical training provided by specialists
results.description:
Executive Summary:

During 2025, the Science and Scaling for Impact Program (S4I) implemented a capacity development strategy to accelerate the adoption of sustainable technologies in Mexico, Guatemala, and Honduras. The strategy combined hands-on field training, demonstration modules, extension areas, and digital tools, using participatory methodologies aimed at strengthening evidence-based decision-making at the territorial level. In 2025, 78,602 farmers in Mexico and Guatemala were trained through short courses covering technical and socio-development topics prioritized according to local needs. In Quintana Roo, an additional 40 community leaders were trained through a hybrid, gamified course supported by WhatsApp-based follow-up. As part of the digital component, micro-courses were delivered via WhatsApp, resulting in 243 people completing at least one online course (43% women). Capacity was also strengthened among key actors supporting technical advisory services: 15 trainers were trained in Oaxaca (6 hours), and 30 change agents completed their training process in Quintana Roo. Within the certification component, the Sustainable Agriculture Certified Technician program (TC-AS) graduated 40 technicians in 2025: 13 in Guatemala, 6 in Honduras, 13 in GRUMA, and 8 in Heineken Mexico, consolidating a network of technicians with the skills to promote sustainable innovations and support scaling efforts in strategic territories.

results.title: Groundwater must be fully integrated into WASH programmes to make them climate resilient
results.description: Groundwater is a critical source of freshwater that provides nearly half of global  drinking water. Its comparative resilience to weather and climatic extremes, particularly drought, makes it essential to water security across agricultural, industrial, and  ecological systems around the world [1–4].  In the Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) sector, groundwater is the predominant source of water for WASH services, especially in rural and low, middle-income  settings (LMICs). Its prominence is driven, in part, by its widespread distribution  and general resilience [5]. Yet, groundwater is not only a source for WASH services  but impacted by them, both from contamination and overexploitation, highlighting a  complex interdependent relationship. However, despite groundwater’s fundamental  importance, understanding and accounting for groundwater has long been an ‘invisible’ component in WASH programming and wider development planning – sidelined  as a water resources issue instead of being core to ensuring sustainable service  delivery [1,3,6].  As the WASH sector prioritizes climate resilience, this disconnect— as we noted in discussions at the 2024 UNC Water & Health Conference - is increasingly import ant to address. A recent, and welcomed, definition of climate-resilient WASH ser vices [7] highlights the need for systems that can anticipate, respond to, cope with, and recover from climate-related events. Yet how can we ensure these goals are met if the underlying water resource for WASH services is poorly understood, not accounted for, and inconsistently managed? We argue that without integration – not  just coordination - of groundwater into WASH programming, the climate-resilient  WASH vision risks being aspirational rather than achievable.

results.title: Hits and misses: water-based climate change adaptation interventions for agriculture in South Asia
results.description:
South Asia's small and marginal farmers are vulnerable to climate change. This is a pressing concern due to the region's heavy dependence on agriculture. There is an urgent need to invest in adaptations that are effective. This study conducts an in-depth analysis of climate change adaptation interventions in the context of South Asia's unique challenges.

In this meta-review of existing literature, we evaluated 70 selected papers focused on water-related climate adaptations in the agriculture sector in South Asia. Our analysis highlights both positive outcomes and unintended consequences. We found that interventions focusing on on-farm practices and water management showed positive impacts on productivity and livelihoods. However, many adaptation interventions did not consider environmental sustainability or equity enough. Notably, the study shows that much of the burden of adaptation fell on farmers. Interventions entailed behaviour change but were accompanied by relatively little policy or financing support.

To achieve farm-scale adaptation, enabling policies and support for social structures are essential. At the watershed scale, water accounting is crucial to avoid scale-related unintended consequences. Finally, mainstreaming adaptation through development projects can enhance effectiveness, in settings where farmers are still poor.

results.title: Dinámica de los bosques en territorios que transitan entre el conflicto y la construcción de paz: Un análisis espacial con enfoque territorial en municipios de Antioquia priorizados por el Acuerdo en Colombia
results.description:
This publication is the result of the doctoral research conducted by the first author as part of her PhD in Animal Sciences at the University of Antioquia. The study integrates multiple methodological approaches to analyze the factors driving deforestation—considering not only traditional biophysical and economic aspects but also human dimensions—at a local scale in municipalities prioritized under Colombia’s peace agreement.

Drawing on this knowledge and reflecting on the broader peacebuilding context, the work explores the enabling conditions for a future scenario of forest conservation in these territories.

This book also includes contributions from faculty experts in rural extension and forest engineering, who authored a chapter on teaching approaches in forestry education in Mexico, offering insights and reflections relevant to the Colombian context. Through this collaboration, the role of universities is acknowledged as fundamental in shaping individuals committed to ecosystem and forest preservation, thereby strengthening their contribution to sustainable development in Latin America.

results.title: Factors influencing the performance of multidisciplinary working groups in delivering climate information services to agro-pastoralists in Senegal: Insights from structural topic modelling
results.description: This report evaluates the resilience of Senegal’s pastoral systems through improved Climate Information Services (CIS). The assessment covered pastoral communities in Ndame, Oudalaye, and Yarang Balante, examining CIS access, use, and the effectiveness of Multidisciplinary Working Groups (MWGs). Results show that pastoralists value CIS for managing drought, pasture scarcity, and livestock health risks, but major constraints limit impact. Low literacy, weak connectivity, gender disparities, and poorly localized or untimely forecasts reduce usability. MWGs play a critical intermediary role but face challenges related to resources, coordination, and sustainability. Pastoralists demonstrate strong adaptive practices, including transhumance and collective grazing, yet these remain fragmented. The core challenge lies in CIS delivery rather than demand. Enhancing impact requires co-produced, human-centered CIS embedded in pastoral realities. Key recommendations include localizing information, strengthening gender and youth inclusion, integrating CIS with livestock services, institutionalizing MWGs, and expanding digital and radio dissemination to support long-term adaptation.

results.title: Finanzas y educación financiera - Virgen del Carmen
results.description: Thirty-six producers in Virgen del Carmen participated in this May 2024 financial education training delivered through CEDRO's partnership. The four-hour session covered financial planning fundamentals, household budgeting, savings habits, credit evaluation, and investment decision-making for farm and family welfare. Participants learned to analyze income and expenses, develop spending plans, build savings buffers, assess borrowing options, and make informed financial choices. This capacity building equipped producers with practical financial management skills enabling better stewardship of organic cacao income, planning for productive investments, and building household economic security. The training positioned Virgen del Carmen producers to maximize benefits from premium cacao markets through disciplined financial practices, supporting improved livelihoods and farm business sustainability in Peru's regenerative agriculture territories.

results.title: Unlocking Senegal’s dairy potential: The role of improved feed and stabling practices
results.description:
Dairy demand in Senegal exceeds domestic supply, despite the country’s large cattle herd and significant potential to expand production. To realize this potential, however, challenges related to low productivity, seasonal fluctuations, and limited market linkages must be addressed. 
This study analyzes the effects of introducing improved cowpea forage and sheltering practices on milk production and revenues among agropastoral producers in the Louga and Thiès regions, using quantitative simulations within a System Dynamics model. Results indicate that improved forage enhances milk output throughout the year, including during the dry season and sheltering can help improve it further. 
However, it is important to note that the improve forage grown must cover the needs for the entire dry season, else the cost of purchased feed may outweigh the benefits in increased productivity. Improved market access is also essential for translating milk productivity gains into higher revenues, particularly in areas where marketing opportunities remain limited.


Au Sénégal, la demande en produits laitiers dépasse l'offre nationale, malgré l'important cheptel bovin du pays et son potentiel significatif d'expansion de la production. Pour exploiter ce potentiel, il faut toutefois relever les défis liés à la faible productivité, aux fluctuations saisonnières et aux liens commerciaux limités. 
Cette étude analyse les effets de l'introduction de pratiques améliorées en matière de fourrage à base de niébé et d'abris sur la production laitière et les revenus des producteurs agro-pastoraux des régions de Louga et de Thiès, à l'aide de simulations quantitatives dans un modèle de dynamique des systèmes. Les résultats indiquent que l'amélioration du fourrage augmente la production laitière tout au long de l'année, y compris pendant la saison sèche, et que l'abri peut contribuer à l'améliorer davantage.
Il est toutefois important de noter que le fourrage amélioré cultivé doit couvrir les besoins pendant toute la saison sèche, sinon le coût des aliments achetés pourrait l'emporter sur les avantages liés à l'augmentation de la productivité. L'amélioration de l'accès au marché est également essentielle pour traduire les gains de productivité laitière en revenus plus élevés, en particulier dans les régions où les débouchés commerciaux restent limités.
